analysis.one_liner: Eliminates qualified immunity, letting people sue police officers for constitutional violations.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in the Senate and sent to the Judiciary Committee, where it has received no hearing, no vote, and no action beyond one cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: When a police officer violates someone's constitutional rights — for example, using excessive force — courts have allowed the officer to escape liability under a doctrine called qualified immunity, unless the victim can show the exact conduct was already ruled illegal in a prior case. This bill would change federal law so that a police officer can no longer use that defense in a civil lawsuit. The change would apply to federal, state, and local law enforcement officers, and would cover lawsuits already pending or filed after the bill becomes law.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people harmed by police misconduct — including federal law enforcement conduct, which current law does not reach through this statute — would gain a clear path to sue officers and recover damages without having to find an earlier case that declared the same conduct illegal. Victims' families and civil-rights plaintiffs would be the direct beneficiaries.

how_it_helps.text: The bill adds a provision to the federal civil-rights statute (42 U.S.C. 1983) stating that an officer's good faith, honest belief, or the absence of clearly established law can no longer be used as a defense. [S2]
It extends liability to federal law enforcement officers acting under federal authority, a gap that the existing statute does not cover. [S2]
The change applies to lawsuits pending on, or filed after, the date of enactment. [S2]

analysis.who_pays: Law enforcement officers, who would face personal financial liability in civil-rights lawsuits, and the cities, states, and federal government that would face more litigation and higher judgments or settlement costs. Police unions and municipal insurers would also bear increased exposure.

drawbacks.text: Removing qualified immunity could expose individual officers to personal ruinous judgments for split-second decisions, and critics argue this makes it harder to recruit and retain police; courts adopted the doctrine partly to shield officers from the burden of litigation over reasonable mistakes. [S2]
Municipalities and taxpayers would absorb higher litigation and settlement costs from a larger volume of lawsuits against police. [S2]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill creates a genuine remedy for people whose constitutional rights are violated by police, including a class of federal officers currently unreachable by the statute, and it does so by removing a judicially created defense rather than creating new crimes. The honest cost is that individual officers and their employers would face substantially more civil liability, which supporters see as deterrence and opponents see as a burden on police work and local budgets. The bill leaves indemnification arrangements untouched, meaning in practice governments, not officers, would often pay — which is a fair criticism of its design from either direction.

outcome.mechanism: Senator Markey introduced the bill and it was sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which has not taken it up.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the Senate on January 13, 2026. [S1]
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day, with no further action in the record since. [S4]
The bill has one cosponsor, a Democrat, alongside its Democratic sponsor. [S3]

The bill text amends the federal civil-rights statute to bar the qualified-immunity defenses of good faith, reasonable belief, and lack of clearly established law, and to cover federal law enforcement officers. [S2]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Law enforcement officers and police unions are better off so far: without a committee hearing or floor vote, the qualified-immunity defense remains intact. No one else has gained anything from the bill's current status.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Police unions and officers, for now

for.name: Sen. Edward Markey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Qualified Immunity Abolition Act of 2026 in the Senate.

for.name: Unnamed Democratic senator
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's sole cosponsor.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and has taken no action — no hearing, markup, or vote — since January 13, 2026.

sides.party_line_note: Both supporters are Democrats; no Republican has cosponsored, and with Republicans holding the Senate majority and chairing Judiciary, the bill has not moved.

industries.industry: Law enforcement officers and police unions
industries.note: The bill strips away the qualified-immunity defense that currently shields officers from personal liability in civil-rights lawsuits, exposing them to suits from people they harm. Police unions have historically opposed ending qualified immunity because it removes their members' protection from damages.

Cities, counties, and states would face more lawsuits and higher settlement and judgment costs, and in practice often indemnify officers, meaning taxpayers would absorb much of the cost. Governments would also gain clearer accountability standards for their police forces.

Ending qualified immunity would make civil-rights cases substantially easier to bring and win, expanding work for lawyers who represent victims of police misconduct. Their interest runs alongside the people they would represent.

analysis.trajectory: With a single cosponsor, no Republican support, and no committee action since referral, the bill is very unlikely to get a hearing or a vote in this Congress. It will most likely sit in the Judiciary Committee until the session ends.
